evidence.note: Lean proofs of local smoothing for all n ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ p < ∞, Bochner–Riesz, spherical extension, Stein square function, the Kakeya maximal estimate and full Kakeya dimension. The paraboloid, cone, Schrödinger and Nikodym results are not in the scope note.

headline: A claimed proof of Sogge's local smoothing conjecture in every dimension, implying full-dimensional Kakeya sets.
scope: The claim covers the Euclidean half-wave for every n ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ p < ∞. It allows every positive loss above the sharp order. The lossless estimate is claimed only at p = 2.
plain: A wave can briefly pile up its energy where its rays meet. So its size at one instant can be worse than its start. Averaging over a short stretch of time is conjectured to win back most of that loss. Sogge's conjecture says exactly how much is won back in each Lᵖ size measure. This paper claims the conjecture in every space dimension, with Bochner–Riesz, Fourier restriction and Kakeya results as consequences.
doesNot: This does not prove the lossless estimate for p > 2, or local smoothing on curved manifolds.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Christopher Sogge, who introduced local smoothing
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles local smoothing in every dimension and implies the Bochner–Riesz and Kakeya conjectures.

explanation:
Take an initial wave f(x) = sin(Nx) with frequency N = 1000. Its derivative has size about N. A fractional derivative of order α scales it by about N^α. That is how Sobolev size measures smoothness. The Lᵖ norm is the p-th root of the integral of |f|ᵖ. At one fixed time, a wave in n space dimensions can need (n − 1)(1/2 − 1/p) extra derivatives in Lᵖ size[3]. In three dimensions at p = 3 that is 2 × 1/6 = 1/3. For N = 1000 that costs a factor of about 1000^(1/3) = 10.

A wave from a thin spherical shell can pile up where its rays meet. Sogge asked how many derivatives you need when you also average over a short time interval[6]. His conjecture says the order drops to just above s₊(p) = max{0, (n − 1)/2 − n/p}. At n = 3 and p = 3, that is max{0, 1 − 1} = 0. So only an arbitrarily small loss should remain. A loss of 0.01 costs about 1000^0.01 ≈ 1.07, instead of 10. At n = 4 and p = 4, the fixed-time order is 3/4 and s₊ is 1/2. The gain is 1/4, which is 1/p. For p at or above 2n/(n − 1), the conjecture asks for every gain below 1/p[4].

Earlier work reached parts of this. Wolff got every gain below 1/p for p > 74 in the plane[7]. Bourgain and Demeter's decoupling theorem gave it for p ≥ 2(n + 1)/(n − 1) in every dimension[8]. In the plane, Guth, Wang and Zhang reached the critical exponent p = 4[9]. At n = p = 3, Gao, Liu, Miao and Xi got every gain below 2/9, against the conjectured 1/3[10]. Gan, He, Li and Wu proved nearly the full gain for p ≥ 10/3[21]. That gives every gain below 1/4 at p = 3[11]. A September 2026 paper in this family claimed the three-dimensional case[19].

The October paper claims the estimate for every n ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ p < ∞, with any loss ε > 0 above s₊(p)[1]. At p = 2 no loss is needed[2]. A focusing wave shows that s₊(p) cannot be lowered[5]. The proof rests on one estimate at the critical exponent p = 2n/(n − 1)[17]. The word Euclidean matters. Some curved three-dimensional spaces need p ≥ 10/3 for gains close to 1/p[18].

Several old problems follow. Bochner–Riesz means rebuild a function from its frequencies with a softened cut-off. They are bounded in the conjectured range for 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞[12]. Fourier extension estimates from the sphere hold in the whole interior of their conjectured range[13]. The Kakeya maximal conjecture follows, with loss δ^(−ε) for tubes of radius δ[14]. So every set in ℝⁿ with a unit line segment in each direction has full Hausdorff dimension n[15]. Before this, Davies had proved it in the plane, and Wang and Zahl in three dimensions[16].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked the main estimate for every n ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ p < ∞. It has also checked the Bochner–Riesz bounds, spherical extension, the Stein square-function bound, the Kakeya maximal estimate and full Kakeya dimension. The Lean scope note links each of these to a fixed reference statement. The paraboloid, cone, Schrödinger and Nikodym results are not in the Lean scope note. No independent review of the proof has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if the proof holds, since it settles local smoothing in every dimension and full Kakeya dimension. Lean checks the main estimate and five consequences. No independent review is published.

glossary.meaning: A gain in smoothness for a wave when its size is averaged over a short time interval.
The number of derivatives an estimate gives up, measured by powers of the frequency.
A measure of a function's size: the p-th root of the integral of its absolute value to the power p.
A piece of a wave concentrated along a thin tube in one direction.
An inequality that bounds a sum of wave pieces using their separate sizes.
Ways to rebuild a function from its frequencies with a softened cut-off at the edge of a ball.
A set that contains a unit line segment pointing in every direction.
A measure of how much space a set fills, which can be a fraction for rough sets.

claims.text: For n ≥ 2, 2 ≤ p < ∞ and ε > 0, the half-wave obeys the local smoothing bound with Sobolev order s₊(p) + ε.
claims.sourceLine: For \(n\ge2\), \(2\le p<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\),
claims.sourceQuote: For \(n\ge2\), \(2\le p<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), \begin{equation}\label{eq:sogge} \|U(T)f\|_{L^p(\RR^n\times I)} \le C_{n,p,\varepsilon}\|J^{s_+(p)+\varepsilon} f\|_{L^p(\RR^n)} . \end{equation}

claims.text: At p = 2 one can take ε = 0.
claims.sourceLine: At \(p=2\) one can take \(\varepsilon=0\).
claims.sourceQuote: At \(p=2\) one can take \(\varepsilon=0\).

claims.text: At a fixed nonzero time the sharp Sobolev order is (n−1)(1/2 − 1/p).
claims.sourceLine: At a fixed nonzero time the sharp Sobolev order is
claims.sourceQuote: At a fixed nonzero time the sharp Sobolev order is \((n-1)(1/2-1/p)\) \cite{Peral1980,Miyachi1980,SSS1991}.

claims.text: For p ≥ 2n/(n−1), averaging in time gains every amount less than 1/p.
claims.sourceLine: Thus for \(p\ge\pc=2n/(n-1)\), averaging in time gains every amount
claims.sourceQuote: Thus for \(p\ge\pc=2n/(n-1)\), averaging in time gains every amount less than \(1/p\) over the fixed-time estimate.

claims.sourceLine: that \(s_+(p)\) is the smallest possible threshold
claims.sourceQuote: A focusing wave shows that \(s_+(p)\) is the smallest possible threshold (Proposition~\ref{prop:sharpness}).

claims.sourceQuote: Sogge asked how many derivatives of the initial data are needed to control the norm averaged over a time interval \cite[Section~4, Equation~(4.5)]{Sogge1991}.
